newsitem.title: USA: Cotton farmers go high-tech with online marketing.
newsitem.headline: Cotton farmers go high-tech with online marketing.

text.p: In an attempt to keep pace with the increasingly high-tech world of agriculture, the National Cotton Council (NCC) has launched the first online risk management tool for farmers.

The software creates various fundamental market scenarios to help growers make decisions on a range of risk factors. It contains end-of-the-day futures and options activity, world price data, reports on risk management, and historic relationships between world prices and New York futures, on a single site.
Farmers can use daily values for soybeans, corn and wheat, for example, to gauge their return on cotton compared with other crops.

"Growers can find this information in pieces and parts but they won't find it completely intergrated into a database with graphics capability and the ability to take futures and cash prices and bring them onto one chart," Mark Lange, an economist with the NCC, said. "This software is unique."
He said the range of information offered through the software makes the program useful to both the "first timer and the master marketer."

One of the more sophisticated features is a price model that provides growers with a current benchmark world cotton price, and identifies factors that have historically explained 95 percent of cotton price behavior.

Marketing sources said such a program is necessary under the Federal Agriculture Improvement and Reform Act (FAIR) of 1996, which put a cap on government subsidies to farmers and removed restrictions on which crops farmers may grow. Such flexibility will lead to volatility in futures markets while making growers more vulnerable to price swings, industry sources said.
"We now have farm legislation that has the market be more of a signal maker for producers regarding what is planted and the resources allocated," Lange said.
Despite an easy-to-use, menu-driven format, critics say cotton growers will resist the new marketing tool, adding that many do not own a home computer.
The marketing service is available to NCC members on CD-Rom or through the organization's home page (http://www.cotton.org).
The program was funded by Zeneca Ag Products and the New York Cotton Exchange (NYCE).
